# 47 CFR § 15.107 - Conducted limits.
(a) Except for Class A digital devices, for equipment that is designed to be connected to the public utility (AC) power line, the radio frequency voltage that is conducted back onto the AC power line on any frequency or frequencies within the band 150 kHz to 30 MHz shall not exceed the limits in the following table, as measured using a 50 μH/50 ohms line impedance stabilization network (LISN).
(d) Measurements to demonstrate compliance with the conducted limits are not required for devices which only employ battery power for operation and which do not operate from the AC power lines or contain provisions for operation while connected to the AC power lines. Devices that include, or make provision for, the use of battery chargers which permit operating while charging, AC adaptors or battery eliminators or that connect to the AC power lines indirectly, obtaining their power through another device which is connected to the AC power lines, shall be tested to demonstrate compliance with the conducted limits.

| 4.5 | 50 Ω/5 μH + 1 Ω V-AMN | 150 kHz to 108 MHz | Low-impedance supplies, for example vehicle and high-current set-ups |

| 4.7 | 150 Ω delta-network (Δ-AMN) | 150 kHz to 30 MHz | Measures symmetric and asymmetric voltages separately |

Source: CISPR 16-1-2:2014, table of contents and clause 4. The "typical use" column is ours; the product standard decides which network applies.

A note under clause 4.3 adds that a network meeting the combined impedance requirements of 4.3 and 4.4 can also be used from 150 kHz to 30 MHz, which is why many commercial LISN models are sold as "50 Ω/50 μH + 5 Ω, 9 kHz to 30 MHz". The 50 Ω/50 μH + 5 Ω characteristic itself is specified only up to 150 kHz.

### What the impedance requirement says

- Impedance is specified in magnitude and phase, measured at an EUT terminal against the reference ground with the receiver port terminated in 50 Ω (clause 4.2).
- It must hold "for any value of external impedance, including a short circuit" at the mains terminal, at all temperatures the network reaches, for continuous currents up to the rated maximum and for peak currents up to the specified maximum (clause 4.2). A network driven past its peak-current rating by inrush or by a capacitor-input rectifier no longer gives a valid measurement.

jina.title: CE102 — Conducted Emissions Testing
jina.snippet:
## Overview

### Purpose

The [MIL-STD-461](https://www.emisleuth.com/emc-test-methods/mil-std-461/)**CE102** test method measures conducted emission noise on the power leads of electronic units. Unlike FCC testing which only applies to AC power inputs, CE102 applies to both AC and DC power inputs. The purpose is to ensure a high quality of power supplied by the bus and limit noise seen by connected units. Because power lines are typically unshielded, it also limits electric field coupling to nearby sensitive analog circuits.

**Frequency coverage comparison:**

| Test | Frequency Range | Comment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CE101 | 30 Hz - 20 kHz |  |
| **CE102** | **10 kHz – 10 MHz** | **<- Discussed here** |
| CS101 | 30 Hz – 150 kHz |  |
| CS114 | 10 kHz – 200 MHz | Includes power line noise at high frequency |

### CE102 Limit Line

The standard CE102 limit line for AC and DC powered units with a 50 µH LISN is defined for noise from **10 kHz to 10 MHz**. For comparison, FCC testing covers 150 kHz to 30 MHz. Satellite EMC requirements often extend the 60 dBµV limit to 20 or 50 MHz.

> **Note:**  
> All limit levels are RMS —> 60 dBµV = 1 mVrms = 1.414 mVpk

![Image 1: MIL-STD-461G Figure CE102-1. CE102 Limit (EUT power leads, AC and DC) for all applications.](https://www.emisleuth.com/images/MIL-STD-461G_Figure_CE102-1_Limit_Line.png)

### CE102 Test Setup

The standard setup requires:

*   Test harnesses minimum **3 meters** long
*   Power and communication lines to separate connectors with **minimum 2 cm separation**
*   50 µH LISN connected per the standard diagram
*   Measurement receiver (spectrum analyzer or oscilloscope for pre-compliance)

linkup.snippet:
## What conducted emissions measure  
[Section titled “What conducted emissions measure”](#what-conducted-emissions-measure)  
The FCC rule gives the cleanest definition of the quantity: compliance "shall be based on the measurement of the radio frequency voltage between each power line and ground at the power terminal" (47 CFR 15.107(a)), on any frequency in the band 150 kHz to 30 MHz, measured with a 50 μH/50 ohm LISN. CISPR 32 sets its AC mains port limits over the same band and in the same unit, dB(μV).  
Why 150 kHz? The FCC explained it when it moved its own limits down from 450 kHz to 150 kHz in 2002: the change brought harmonisation with CISPR 22 and protects licensed services below 450 kHz, the Report and Order citing Differential GPS beacons between 285 and 325 kHz used for safety-of-life navigation. Why 30 MHz? The same order states that the conducted limits "protect against interference to licensed radio services operating below 30 MHz"; above that, radiated emission limits take over.
### What the impedance requirement says

seltz.title: Conducted emissions: LISN method, CISPR and FCC limits
seltz.snippet:
Conducted emissions are the radio-frequency voltage a product pushes back onto its power lead. The European and US regimes both limit it from 150 kHz to 30 MHz, measured through a LISN (Line Impedance Stabilisation Network, which CISPR calls a V-network artificial mains network). This page goes back to the texts: which network CISPR 16-1-2 actually specifies for which band, the CISPR 32 and 47 CFR 15.107 limit tables side by side, what the FCC detector rule allows, which EN 55032 version the EU list cites in October 2026, and the common readings the texts contradict. It is written for product engineers preparing an EMC campaign and for project managers who need to know why a bench result is not a lab result.

The FCC rule gives the cleanest definition of the quantity: compliance "shall be based on the measurement of the radio frequency voltage between each power line and ground at the power terminal" (47 CFR 15.107(a)), on any frequency in the band 150 kHz to 30 MHz, measured with a 50 μH/50 ohm LISN. CISPR 32 sets its AC mains port limits over the same band and in the same unit, dB(μV).

Why 150 kHz? The FCC explained it when it moved its own limits down from 450 kHz to 150 kHz in 2002: the change brought harmonisation with CISPR 22 and protects licensed services below 450 kHz, the Report and Order citing Differential GPS beacons between 285 and 325 kHz used for safety-of-life navigation. This article summarizes the webinar strategy, from the measurement set-up and mode separation to the design of an optimized single-stage line filter, its safety limits and its installation, for design engineers who need to bring a switch-mode power supply below the conducted emission limits.

The webinar by Würth Elektronik, presented by Lorandt Foelkel and Marco from Emzer, explains where to use a power line filter and a common mode choke and how to choose an optimum filter by separating differential-mode (DM) and common-mode (CM) noise [1]. It combines a theoretical introduction with live experiments on a flyback power supply that fails the test without a filter. The article adds the calculation procedure from the related Würth Elektronik application note [2] and the applicable limits. ## Overview

### Purpose

The MIL-STD-461 **CE102** test method measures conducted emission noise on the power leads of electronic units. Unlike FCC testing which only applies to AC power inputs, CE102 applies to both AC and DC power inputs. The purpose is to ensure a high quality of power supplied by the bus and limit noise seen by connected units. Because power lines are typically unshielded, it also limits electric field coupling to nearby sensitive analog circuits.

**Frequency coverage comparison:**


| Test | Frequency Range | Comment |
| ---- | --------------- | ------- |
| CE101 | 30 Hz - 20 kHz |  |
| **CE102** | **10 kHz – 10 MHz** | **<- Discussed here** |

| CS114 | 10 kHz – 200 MHz | Includes power line noise at high frequency |

The standard CE102 limit line for AC and DC powered units with a 50 µH LISN is defined for noise from **10 kHz to 10 MHz**. For comparison, FCC testing covers 150 kHz to 30 MHz. Satellite EMC requirements often extend the 60 dBµV limit to 20 or 50 MHz.
